craft_claim: Fluent sound- and rhythm-patterning produces positive aesthetic affect because processing ease is misattributed to the language itself, which is the felt engine of the lyrical tone.

supporting_evidence.location: Personality and Social Psychology Review 8(4):364-382, theoretical synthesis and aesthetic-pleasure model
supporting_evidence.note: Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman argue that the ease of processing a stimulus is experienced as positive affect and misattributed to the stimulus; fluency is raised by repetition, prototypicality, symmetry, and clarity of form.
Rhyming statements were rated more truthful and apt than matched non-rhyming paraphrases, showing that phonetic fluency is read as a property of the statement.

counterevidence.note: Fluency effects depend on context and expectation; high disfluency can lower liking, and the authors caution against treating fluency as a universal cause of pleasure.
Deviation and foregrounding also produce positive affect, so novel difficulty is not uniformly disliked; the fluency account is one mechanism among several.

scope: All lyrical prose and verse; strongest where lexical content is already understood and the reader is attending to form.
exceptions: Texts whose purpose requires maximal disfluency or estrangement (some experimental and political poetics).
Audiences reading in a second language, where the fluency signal is unreliable.
